sentiment.instructions: Judge the overall sentiment the author expresses in this short social-media post (tweet), considering tone, emotion, and attitude toward the topic, events, or people mentioned. Ignore incidental words like 'may', ordinal dates, or event names unless they carry feeling.

positive.description: The author conveys happiness, excitement, anticipation, praise, admiration, affection, gratitude, well-wishes, or celebration (e.g., looking forward to an event, calling something the best, greetings like happy holidays, condolences/prayers offered warmly, promoting something enthusiastically).
examples: Not even 20 pages into Paper Towns and the book centers around the night of May 5th. I know its gonna be a good one now!

neutral.description: The post mainly shares information, news, announcements, questions, logistics, or casual observations without clear positive or negative emotion; mild jokes or mixed/ambiguous remarks with no dominant feeling also count.
examples: I may be sleep deprived but I promise you that some kid at Dunkin today looked like a sprout.

negative.description: The author conveys disappointment, annoyance, anger, sadness, boredom, criticism, insults, mockery, sarcasm, complaints, inability to attend something, or hostility toward a person, group, or situation.
examples: The tragedy of only thinking up hilarious tweets for the Summer Olympics now is that in four years there may be no place for them.
